extracted.intended_audience: orators, writers, and students of rhetoric (practitioners of elevated prose and verse)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing ‘sublime’ elevated style in oratory and poetry — how to employ images, figures of speech, diction, and structural devices to achieve grandeur, energy, and emotional effect while avoiding excess and artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate the great models / fix an eye of rivalry on high examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When labouring on a subject demanding a lofty and majestic style, imagine how Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides, etc., would have expressed it; let such high examples be beacons to guide and lift up the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rivalry with great predecessors as incentive and model; imagine how those judges or an audience of heroes would criticise or be affected by your work to spur exertion and raise standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate judgment of future ages while staying intelligible to contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask 'With what feelings will future ages through all time read these my works?' but beware that fear of being unintelligible to contemporaries will make conceptions crude and lacking perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for enduring perfection, yet ensure clarity for present readers so your thought is not maimed by over-ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and employ images to work on the emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Image (in broad sense) includes any thought issuing in speech; more narrowly, when the speaker, rapt with feeling, imagines what he speaks of and produces a similar illusion in hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both poets and orators use images to affect emotion; cultivate the ability to make hearers 'see' what you describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetical vs. oratorical images
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetical image is designed to astound; the oratorical image to give perspicuity; both affect the emotions but with different ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use poetic imagination where astonishment is sought; in oratory, prefer images that clarify and strengthen argument rather than impossible or monstrous fables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mythical exaggeration and impossibility in oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythical exaggeration is allowable in poetry but becomes offensive and monstrous in oratory when language runs into impossibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep oratorical images grounded and real; excessive fable-like imagery undermines persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate images with argument to enthrall as well as convince
rubrics_metrics.description: An oratorical image mingled with the practical, argumentative parts of an oration does not merely convince, but enthralls the hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy striking images amid proofs to carry logical objection before you by affecting audience emotions and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sublimity and passion to disguise rhetorical artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech tend to arouse suspicion of dishonesty; when associated with sublimity and passion, their artifice is overshadowed and becomes invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate genuine grandeur and fervour so that figures appear natural and their artificial character is obscured by brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures judiciously to produce sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, judiciously employed, play an important part in producing sublimity; reckless or unmeasured use is dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select figures for their appropriateness to occasion and avoid indiscriminate ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ Apostrophe / adjuration to exalt and rouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjuration (apostrophe) — sudden exalted address (e.g., 'I swear it by the men who faced the foe at Marathon') — raises the hearer to heroic pride and can command assent by startling novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adjuration at the right place, manner, occasion, and motive to elevate emotion and strengthen appeal; it is the context and handling that confer grandeur, not the oath itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure language in inspired moments to avoid giving opponents a handle
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in inspired exultation the orator must 'measure his language, choosing his very words so as to give no handle to opponents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft exalted utterances with care — omit potentially damaging words (e.g., avoid 'conquered') or qualify phrases to prevent critics from exploiting your rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary that figures can provoke distrust or seem sophistical
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures have a tendency to rouse suspicion of treachery or false reasoning, especially before judges or rulers who may feel patronised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disguise artifice with genuine passion and grandeur; avoid obvious artifice that treats listeners as fools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetorical question and interrogation to stir and energise
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of question and interrogation, especially when the orator replies to himself, stir an audience and give energy, simulating meeting objections and reproducing the moment of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate question and answer to mimic debate and startle audiences into immediate, emotionally charged assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use asyndeton (removal of connecting particles) for rapid rush
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of connecting particles gives a quick rush and 'torrent rapture' to a passage (e.g., 'they pushed, they fought, they slew, they fell').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply asyndeton to create urgency and breathless movement, especially in distressed or impassioned passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine different figures for amplified vigour
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of different figures — two or three uniting — mutually contribute to vigour, cogency, and beauty of a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer devices (repetition, inversion, asyndeton, interrogation, etc.) to produce cumulative force, as Demosthenes does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and broken clauses to imitate action and agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating words and breaking up sentences (broken clauses) produce lively, disorderly movement that imitates passion and agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary rhythm with repetition and abrupt clauses to keep speech from standing still and to simulate the speaker's emotional state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of conjunctions that curb passion's momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions and connecting links smooth away rapidity; passion rebels against such trammels because they curb free rush and destroy the impression of mechanical impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit conjunctions when representing impetuous feeling; use them when logical order and clarity are the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ hyperbaton (word-order inversion) to convey agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbaton, transposition of words from their usual order, bears the stamp of violent mental agitation and imitates the halting, swerving speech of the distressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversions boldly to create an air of unpremeditated debate or terror; Thucydides and Demosthenes use it to drag the audience into peril.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use juxtaposition, enumeration, contrast, and climax for vigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition of cases, enumeration of particulars, use of contrast and climax add vigour, elevation, and life to style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange particulars and contrasts intentionally to build momentum and emotional intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate number (plural for singular, singular for plural) for rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Using plurals for singulars (or vice versa) can give an impression of vastness or corporate life: plurals may amplify calamity, singulars may condense and dignify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose number to amplify or contract impression according to theme; avoid gratuitous shifts of number except for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the historical present / dramatizing past as present for immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing past events as happening in present time converts narrative into dramatic action and makes readers spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the historic present to increase immediacy and vividness in narrative passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interchange of persons and direct address to place reader in the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct personal address ('thou', second person) or shifting persons makes the reader fancy himself moving in the midst of the perils described and excites interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the individual reader or shift person to rouse interest and fix attention; useful to make the audience partake in the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change person within narrative for explosive passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden transition from third person narrative to first/character speech strikes like an outburst of passion and is appropriate to urgent crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt person change sparingly and where crisis demands immediacy; avoid gratuitous intrusions that would seem forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use periphrasis to lend dignity and melody, but restrain it
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis often lends dignity ('death' as 'destined journey') and harmonises plain speech, yet it is liable to abuse, soon becoming feeble or vapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ periphrasis where it elevates tone; avoid inflated, harsh, or pedantic circumlocution that draws ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate, striking words — 'beautiful words are the very light of thought'
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of appropriate and striking words has marvellous power and enthralling charm; beautiful words endow facts with a vocal soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select diction that matches subject-matter — grand language for lofty themes; avoid applying imposing language to trifling subjects (avoid a 'huge tragic mask on a little child').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use homely/plain language when its vividness suits the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Homely language is sometimes far more vivid than the most ornamental, being immediately recognisable as the language of common life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't spurn plain or colloquial turns if they convey expressiveness (e.g., 'taking doses of trouble'); match register to desired vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of simultaneous metaphors, but follow the occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics advise not more than two or three metaphors combined in the same place; yet impassioned outbursts may demand masses of metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer restraint generally; in torrents of passion allow abundant metaphors provided passion and sublimity carry them and prevent critical pause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soften harsh or daring metaphors with qualifying phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and Theophrastus recommend mitigating bold metaphors by the use of phrases like 'so to say', 'as it were', 'if I may be permitted the expression'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such qualifiers to forestall criticism when a metaphor risks seeming too bold or incongruous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a close, continuous series of metaphors for detailed description
rubrics_metrics.description: In descriptive passages a succession of metaphors (a continuous series) gives distinctness and fine delineation (e.g., anatomical description in Xenophon/Plato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extended metaphor-series in descriptive or anatomical passages to build a vivid, sustained picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise restraint: figures and figurative language have tendency to excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of figurative language, as of all beauties of style, tends towards excess; great restraint is required because intemperate use produces ridicule or feebleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly check for excess; favour natural feeling and unaffected sublimity over ornament for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let passion and native greatness of thought support figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime arises from native greatness of mind, imitation, and employment of images; sublimity lends support to figures, and figures gain power from passion and grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that rhetorical devices are rooted in genuine passion and elevated thought — devices alone cannot create sublimity.
